newsitem.title: CHINA: China's workers lose confidence in Communist Party.
newsitem.headline: China's workers lose confidence in Communist Party.

text.p: Surveys of China's workers have found a sharp fall in the number who believe in the Communist Party and trust in the future of socialism, while more and more are turning to religion.

"A considerable number of party members in their own hearts do not really recognise themselves as party members," said the magazine Modern Ideological Trends in its latest edition available on Monday.
"They have abandoned the realising of communism as their highest ideal," it said. "This is the attitude of a considerable number of workers and this attitude is expanding by the day.
"If this continues the prospects will be dreadful to contemplate," the hardline leftist magazine warned.

It cited a series of official surveys of workers' opinions by the Communist Party secretariat and the All-China Federation of Trade Unions (ACFTU) since 1982 to show swiftly diminishing confidence in communist rule.
A 1982 survey by the party secretariat showed the top ideal among workers was to realise communism, while ensuring a better life for their family came fifth.
By 1996, those positions had been reversed.

A survey by the ACFTU last year showed the number who chose realising communism as their top ideal had slumped to 29.42 percent from 69.9 percent in 1982 and 57.82 percent in 1986. In 1992, the figure had fallen to 42.3 percent.
In 1996, those who put the family first had risen to 40.11 percent, far exceeding those interested in communism.
"At the same time as workers' ideals are diminishing, their belief in religion is rising," the magazine said.
The number of workers who held religious beliefs had risen to 9.4 percent, it said. It did not give a comparison.

Virtually no Chinese worker would admit to religious beliefs after the end of the ultra-leftist 1966-76 Cultural Revolution, when religion was vilified as the opium of the people and the faithful were persecuted.

"Some workers... sincerely believe in some form of religion leading to a reduction in workers' immunity to the worship of money, feudal superstition and other social diseases and poisons," the magazine said.

The survey showed that in 1996 some 53.09 percent believed China could continue along the socialist road but that this would be a very arduous task, a drop of 20.07 percentage points compared with 1991, the magazine said.
Respondents who were pessimisitic or had doubts about the future of socialism increased by 18.23 percentage points.
"Some workers, especially a group of Communist Party members... do not believe in and even go so far as to hold communism and socialist ideals in contempt," it said.

It blamed the failing trust in communism and growing faith in religion on corruption, the weakening of Marxism and the dismissal of two Communist Party leaders in 1987 and 1989 accused of sympathising with student demonstrators.

"Wining and dining at public expense, whoring and gambling and the cases of people such as (Beijing deputy mayor) Wang Baosen who talk about ideals and beliefs but are corrupt" were to blame, it said.

Wang committed suicide in early 1995 after coming under investigation for corruption in a $37 million scandal that saw the downfall of his boss, Beijing party chief Chen Xitong, and several lesser officials.

The magazine also blamed failing state enterprises, saying that by 1995 a total of 6.9 million state workers were receiving no wages or reduced wages. Of 108 million state workers, only 30 million were well off financially, it said.
"The majority of workers do not think they are the biggest beneficiaries of reform," it said.
